overview: This file combines a State Department jacket, U.S. Embassy despatches, departmental transmittal memoranda, and a translated Japanese colonial ordinance concerning narcotics and opium in Taiwan (Formosa). The principal legal enclosure is Taiwan Government General Ordinance No. 71, a comprehensive licensing and enforcement code governing the manufacture, importation, exportation, transit, sale, possession, cultivation, recordkeeping, inspection, and illicit use of narcotics, coca, and Indian hemp. Later despatches examine the persistence of unlicensed opium smoking, a controversial proposal to issue new smokers’ permits, opposition by Taiwanese organizations and the press, intervention by the Japanese central government, scrutiny by the League of Nations, and proposed treatment and anti-smuggling programs.

subfiles.title: Jacket No. 1: Traffic in Narcotics—Formosa and Taiwan
subfiles.about: The jacket identifies the State Department case concerning narcotics traffic in Formosa and Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Jacket cover for case 894A.114 Narcotics/1 bears a printed 1918 date predating the substantive 1930 documents it holds.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 45 transmitting Taiwan narcotics ordinance
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy transmits an English translation of Taiwan Government General Ordinance No. 71 regulating narcotics and their derivatives.
subfiles.summary: Castle forwards Taiwan's translated narcotics ordinance, effective September 25 per the despatch though the text gives December 25, 1929, copied to Treasury and Commerce.

subfiles.title: Translation of Taiwan Government General Ordinance No. 71
subfiles.from: Taiwan Government General; Eizo Ishizuka, Governor General of Taiwan
subfiles.about: The enclosure sets out a comprehensive colonial regulatory system for narcotics, coca, and Indian hemp in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance defines controlled drugs and restricts their use principally to medicine and science, with permits required for manufacture, foreign and Japan-bound trade, transit, sale, possession, coca cultivation, and certain nonmedical uses. It prescribes labeling, locked storage, detailed registers, annual reports, bonded warehousing, inspections, reporting of theft and addiction, treatment of addicted persons, and official power to limit production or cultivation. Articles 36–42 establish imprisonment, penal servitude, detention, and fines for violations, while the supplementary provisions repeal the 1920 morphine and cocaine ordinance and preserve qualifying earlier permits. The text is dated December 15, 1929 and specifies an effective date of December 25, 1929.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 45 to the Treasury Department
subfiles.about: The State Department sends the Treasury Department a copy of Despatch No. 45 and its translated narcotics ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum transmits the Tokyo Embassy's despatch on Ordinance No. 71, regulating narcotics and derivatives in Taiwan, to the Treasury Department.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 45 to the Commerce Department
subfiles.about: The State Department sends the Commerce Department a copy of Despatch No. 45 and its translated narcotics ordinance.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate memorandum forwards the Embassy despatch and translation of Taiwan Ordinance No. 71 to the Secretary of Commerce.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 61 on proposed opium-smokers’ permits in Taiwan
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports controversy over a Taiwan Government General proposal to issue additional permits to unregistered opium smokers.
subfiles.summary: Castle reviews the permit system established in 1896, reporting 169,064 licensed smokers in 1900, later additions to the rolls, and a decline to about 27,000 registered smokers by the end of 1928 despite fears of growing illicit use. After more than 30,000 people applied for new licenses in December 1929, the Japanese central government halted or postponed their issuance amid press criticism and petitions from Taiwanese organizations. The Cabinet ordered an investigation, contemplated tightly supervised permits, and proposed devoting roughly ¥700,000 in proceeds to treatment and prevention. Castle connects Tokyo’s intervention to the arrival of a League of Nations commission and to international criticism of Japanese narcotics exports to China and India.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 61 to the Treasury Department
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards Treasury a copy of the Embassy report on possible expansion of opium-smokers’ permits in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum transmits Despatch No. 61 reporting Taiwan considered increasing permits issued to opium smokers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 86 on proposed opium-control and treatment program
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr., U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports developing Japanese plans for medical treatment, stricter licensing, and suppression of illicit opium traffic in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Castle reports that widespread secret smoking and evasion of import controls had forced the Japanese government to reconsider its claim that addiction in Taiwan was nearing solution. A proposed policy emphasized medical treatment, permits only for hopeless addicts, renewed examination of existing permit holders, stricter enforcement, and dedication of opium revenue to hospitals and control measures. Press reports anticipated permits for about 5,000 of 25,000 applicants, three-year treatment for more than 20,000 others, expansion of the Saisei-in Hospital at Taihoku, eleven hospital relief stations, seven coastal watch stations, additional officials and approximately 100 special police, and supplementary appropriations of ¥400,000 and ¥100,000. The Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs told the Embassy that final government approval was still pending.

interest: Shows colonial Taiwan's opium-permit system amid diplomatic evidence the formal law understated illicit use.
